speaker_role: independent consultant/marketer (founder of The Scholarship System, a paid scholarship-coaching business)
commercial_incentive: yes - heavily promotes a free webinar and paid programs (The Scholarship System, Debt Free Degree Lab) throughout
key_insights: FAFSA calculates the Student Aid Index (SAI), which replaced the old Expected Family Contribution (EFC); the same SAI number can result in very different aid offers at different schools because each college applies its own institutional policies to it.
Some schools also require the CSS Profile (via College Board) for a deeper look at family finances used for institutional (non-federal) aid, separate from FAFSA.

Individual colleges can set their own FAFSA/CSS Profile deadlines that are earlier than general deadlines, and missing a school-specific priority deadline can mean losing aid entirely even if FAFSA is technically still 'on time' overall.

Financial aid award letters often list loans (which must be repaid) alongside grants/scholarships (which don't), and families should not assume an entire 'award' is debt-free money without checking the breakdown.
Recommends applying to FAFSA about one to two weeks after it opens October 1 rather than immediately, to avoid early-release software bugs while staying within safe timing margins.
Families can appeal a financial aid award if their financial circumstances have materially changed since the FAFSA/CSS data was submitted.

Prioritization order recommended for funding sources: grants and scholarships first, then work-study (noting its hourly pay can sometimes be lower than an outside part-time job), with loans treated as the last resort.
Cites a cautionary anecdote of a family that missed NYU's earlier-than-general FAFSA deadline and was told they would have received about $40,000 more in aid had they submitted on time.
specific_numbers_or_facts: Claims the speaker's company has helped families secure over $16.5 million in scholarships to date (per Jocelyn Penita Pearson, founder)
FAFSA opens October 1 of a student's senior year of high school (per the video)
Anecdote: a family missed NYU's own (earlier) FAFSA deadline and reportedly lost out on approximately $40,000 in aid as a result (per the speaker, unverified specific case)
notable_or_distinctive: Highlights the less commonly emphasized point that individual colleges can impose their own FAFSA/CSS Profile deadlines well ahead of the general FAFSA window, illustrated with a specific high-dollar anecdote (NYU, ~$40,000) rather than only generic 'apply early' advice.
reliability_notes: Delivered as a lead-generation video for a paid scholarship coaching business with a free-webinar call-to-action repeated throughout; the $40,000 NYU anecdote and the $16.5 million company total are unverifiable single-source claims from the speaker.
